Author: brian
Message:
hub-registry: prove the verifier fails, prove revocation works, and make the vetted badge honest (T-3709)

The card said seven features sit inert "because the service they point at
does not exist." The service exists. registry.vnprox.com serves a correctly
signed index with four seed blueprints and their artifacts, stood up by
T-3303 on 2026-08-18; the card was written five days later without knowing.
That is the same failure as the "no cluster" premise — a claim about our own
infrastructure restated from a secondary source and never re-checked. Third
instance, so it is written into the card rather than quietly fixed
(planning/reports/evidence/registry-vnprox-com-2026-08-24.txt).

The real gaps, observed rather than assumed:

  - The name resolves nowhere. NXDOMAIN from the dev box and from pvecube;
    reachable only by sending an explicit Host: header to the IP. That, not
    a missing service, is why the seven features are inert.
  - Both signing keys live only on pve001, which we have no credentials for
    and no authorisation to modify. So we cannot publish an entry, cannot
    rotate, and cannot publish a revocation. The shipped revocation channel
    for the public registry is not unproven — it is inoperable, and
    operators are now told so.
  - GitHub Pages already builds main's root on every push, so the
    GitHub-native registry the owner chose needs no new infrastructure
    (planning/reports/evidence/github-native-hosting-2026-08-24.txt).

scripts/hub-registry-harness.sh builds the real binaries, publishes the
repo's own seed blueprints through the real vnproxctl hub publish/index
pipeline, serves them, and drives a real vnproxd — never a fixture agreeing
with the client that reads it. It demonstrates the half that always gets
skipped: a tampered artifact refused as invalidSignature while the index
stays valid; a tampered index refused whole, with zero entries rather than a
partial catalog; an entry revoked and refused even though its own bundle
signature still verifies; and revocation by signer fingerprint withdrawing
an artifact never named in any revoke, which is the path that matters in a
key compromise.

The vetted badge stops implying a person vouched. internal/hubreg/vetting.go
runs the checks at index time, so the verdict rides inside the signature
everything else is verified against. It does not claim the reproducible-build
check: vnprox has no source-to-artifact pipeline and a plugin artifact never
contains the executable, so there is nothing to rebuild — VetResult carries no
field for it and every result carries a note saying it was not performed. The
badge's hover text says what was actually checked.

Signing custody stays Ed25519 here. Sigstore keyless remains the decision and
is blocked on Actions, which have not run since 2026-08-13.

Author: brian
Message:
compat: build the PVE compatibility matrix from per-version mock profiles (T-2103)

docs/roadmap.md has promised "a compatibility validation task within one phase
of each new PVE release" with no mechanism behind it. This is the mechanism —
the mock-fixture half of it.

Three version profiles (8.2, 9.0, 9.2) and a compat server wrapper that
intercepts only SDN zone creates, gating PVE 9.0's Fabrics zone types
(openfabric/ospf) to the profiles that have them and rejecting them with a
PVE-shaped 400 elsewhere. Everything else passes through the normal mock
untouched. A generator drives real HTTP checks per cell — ticket auth, network
read, a baseline vlan zone, and the gated fabric zone — into docs/
compat-matrix.json and a generated table in docs/compatibility.md, regenerated
by `make compat-matrix` rather than hand-maintained.

AC3 is the one that matters and it is enforced structurally: every cell
carries validation: "mock". docs/compatibility.md says up front that this
whole mechanism is mock-only, points at `vnproxctl telemetry` (T-2503) as the
separate field-validated pathway, and deliberately does NOT fold in the single
real hardware data point this repo has, because a hardware observation sitting
in a mock-generated table is exactly the blur the card forbids.

Verified by mutation at both layers: flipping PVE 8.2's profile to claim
fabric-zone support reddens the unit gate ("status = 200, want 400") AND
TestMatrix_MatchesPublishedArtifact, so a divergence cannot be introduced
without the published artifact disagreeing. Restored, all suites green.

No ci.yml edit was needed — `go test ./...` in the existing check job already
covers the new package. release.yml gains a step that re-runs the suite at
tag time and attaches the stamped matrix; that step is written and locally
exercised but has NEVER run in CI (Actions billing exhausted).

The SDN Fabrics behaviour itself is modelled from documentation, not captured
from hardware: this repo has no PVE 8.2 or 9.0 to observe. Stated in the
fixture and profile comments rather than left to be assumed.

Author: brian
Message:
push: mobile PWA with web push over the existing event stream (T-2005)

RFC 8291 (aes128gcm) and RFC 8292 (VAPID) implemented against the Go standard
library — crypto/ecdh, crypto/ecdsa, crypto/aes — with no new dependency, and
proven byte-for-byte against RFC 8291 Appendix A's worked example rather than
against our own encryptor.

The design decision that matters is what a notification is allowed to contain.
A push lands on a lock screen, so a payload naming a node or a guest leaks the
network's shape to anyone holding the phone. CriticalFindingNotification()
therefore **takes no arguments at all** — Title and Body are fixed literals and
the deep link is /tools?pushCategory=critical, a filtered view, never a
specific finding, because Finding.ID/Detail/Nodes routinely embed node and
guest names. Leakage is prevented by the function having nothing to leak, not
by remembering to redact; the accompanying test is a regression guard with a
positive control leg proving its substring check can actually find an
identifier before asserting none is present. Same discipline internal/telemetry
established for its own payload.

Subscriptions are sealed with the existing SessionCipher and carry
session_id REFERENCES sessions(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, so a subscription dies
with its session structurally rather than via a cleanup hook that can be
forgotten. The service worker never touches /api/* — it checks that first and
does not consult a cache, so an authenticated response cannot be served to the
next user of a shared device.

Migration 0046, with its fixture. Adding it made 45 a prior version rather than
the current latest, so seedV45/assertV45 had to be written too — the corpus
guard fails loudly at setup for any gap in 1..latest-1, and I confirmed it
still does by removing the entry and watching it name the missing version. The
loop itself is untouched.

Consequential edits outside the stated scope, each forced by an existing guard
rather than chosen: a new sealed column needs a backup SecretClass entry or
TestSecretClasses_CoverEverySealedColumn fails, and a new route needs an
apidoc entry or TestOpenAPI_EveryRouteIsDescribed fails.

No [push] config section: the VAPID key path is derived from the blueprint
signing key's directory, which lands it inside --demo's sandbox automatically.
Real configurability (custom path, rotation) is left for a card that needs it.

Verified: go build/vet clean; push, store, api and backup suites green; tsc
clean; 247 files / 1807 frontend tests. Delivery to a real device through
FCM/APNs/autopush, and installability on real iOS/Android, are NOT verified —
everything here runs against synthetic subscriptions and an httptest server.

Author: brian
Message:
demo: one-command install and built-in demo mode (T-2801)

`vnproxd --demo` runs the whole product against a synthetic three-node
cluster embedded in the binary, with no Proxmox VE endpoint and no
outbound network. Evaluating vnprox otherwise requires a cluster, which
is a hard gate in front of every potential user.

Structural, not promised. Three substitutions at the edges, each made by
construction:

  - The PVE client's transport is an in-process http.RoundTripper over
    internal/pvemock (internal/demo/transport.go): no dialer, no socket.
    PVE.APIURL is an RFC 2606 .invalid name, so a path that bypassed it
    would fail to resolve rather than reach localhost:8006 — which on a
    Proxmox node is pveproxy.
  - The host reader is the same fixture, cluster-wide
    (collect.Config.HostServesCluster), and a demo daemon builds no peer
    client at all. Without that, peer fan-out dialled the fixture's own
    10.10.0.x node addresses over the real network.
  - Every mutating API route answers with what it would have done
    (internal/api/demo.go) — a middleware in front of routing, so a route
    added next month is covered by someone who never read that file.

Both directions of the endpoint refusal: config.LoadDemo refuses any
config that sets any [pve] key (ErrDemoRealEndpoint) before a collector
is built, and /federation/clusters and /k8s/clusters are refused
403 demo_real_endpoint_refused rather than answered with a would-have.

The dataset is a checked-in fixture (internal/demo/dataset/), derived
from three-node-vlan with deliberate imperfections enumerated in its own
`mess:` list, plus a flow corpus with relative timestamps replayed
through flow.Service.Ingest.

The installer gains signature verification on every download (the apt
key pinned by fingerprint, the tarball by detached signature), a binary
tarball fallback, an unprivileged --prefix install, and idempotence.
There is no --insecure; a static test asserts the flag cannot appear.
The pinned fingerprint is still a documented placeholder, so downloads
fail closed — there is no published release key to pin.

Fixes a real bug found on the way: the in-process transport leaked the
caller's chi route context into pvemock's router, which reused it and
404'd a login from a route that plainly exists, while every
background-context collector call worked.

Author: brian
Message:
gitsync: open a changeset when the repo and the cluster disagree (T-2701)

A git repository becomes the source of *intent* for internal/spec's
declarative cluster network document. Proxmox stays the source of *truth*:
on each poll the sync fetches one file at one ref, runs the existing
spec.Parse + spec.Import against live inventory, and — if the plan is
non-empty — opens or updates ONE draft changeset and stops. It never
applies.

That is structural, not conventional: the only change-engine surface
internal/gitsync holds is ChangesetStager (CreateWithOrigin/UpdateDraft/
List), which has no Apply/Confirm/Rollback/Discard method at all — the same
interface-surface boundary internal/mcp (T-1701) and internal/plugin
(T-1702) draw. An interface-surface test asserts the omission, and the AC1
test's apply spy ships with a control leg proving the counter it reads moves.

The git-access decision (recorded because the arc's risk register asked for
it explicitly): a plain HTTPS fetch of one file, over net/http. No `git`
binary — the .deb declares no Depends: at all today, and a subprocess whose
argv carries an operator-supplied remote URL is a new injection surface in a
design that pins every external command to a fixed argv. No Go git library —
that is the "large dependency" the register names, an order of magnitude
past the requirement. The consequence is stated rather than hidden in
internal/gitsync/doc.go and docs/security.md: with no object graph, commit
signatures are verified against the commit object the host reports.

Also:
- [gitsync] config, off by default: with no section, nothing is fetched, no
  endpoint contacted, and no credential file read. Credentials live in a
  root:root 0600 token_file, exist only as a request header, and are absent
  from logs/findings/audit/status (one assertion per surface, two controls).
- require_signed_commits verifies git's SSH-format signatures (ed25519,
  rsa-sha2-*) locally against the operator's allowed-signers file, stdlib
  only, failing closed in every direction — never the host's own "verified"
  flag. Fixtures are real: ssh-keygen -Y sign -n git, cross-checked with
  ssh-keygen -Y verify.
- An unreachable remote degrades to a finding plus a retry; Run returns nil
  on cancellation, so it can never take the run group down.
- GET /gitsync/status (+ docs/api.md, docs/openapi.json) and
  `vnproxctl gitsync status`. Read-only: no route or verb triggers a sync or
  applies its draft.
- findings source "gitsync": five detection-only checks.

Description: Identified a GitLab Personal Access Token, risking unauthorized access to GitLab repositories and codebase exposure.
Author: brian
Message:
gitsync: propose a changeset as a pull request against the spec repo (T-2702)

T-2701 made a git repository the source of intent; without this, a change
staged in the vnprox GUI is a change made outside the system of record.
`POST /changesets/{id}/propose` closes the loop: render the changeset as a
spec delta, commit it on a deterministic branch, push, and open a pull
request through the host's API (GitHub and GitLab).

The read and write seams are separate TYPES, not one type with more methods.
`gitsync.Source` (T-2701, read-only) is unchanged and unextended; `Host`
(host.go) is a sibling interface with the branch/commit/pull-request verbs
and no merge, approve, review or poll verb at all. The sync Service holds
only a Source, so "vnprox never pushes on the sync path" is enforced by the
compiler — verified by adding a PushSpec method to Source and watching the
build break in four files. They also hold separate credentials: the push
token is its own key ([gitsync] push_token_file), so a sync-only deployment
never reads a write credential off disk and the route answers 501.

AC1 is enforced in production, not only asserted in a test. Before any host
write, the proposed document must re-import against live state to exactly the
base document's plan plus this changeset's ops — compared semantically (op
ids excluded, ordering excluded, set-valued params compared as sets, the same
equality spec.Import's own diff uses). A changeset the document cannot say
(every delete, and every firewall/IPAM/QoS/WireGuard/raw-file op) is refused
by spec.ApplyOps naming the op; one that would plan to something else is
refused naming the difference.

AC3's ordering: resolve the base, create the branch (remembering whether we
created it), commit, then open or update the request. Any failure past a
branch we created deletes it; a branch that already existed — carrying a
request someone may be reviewing — is never deleted. Verified by removing the
compensating delete and watching six AC3 cases redden.

Also: schema 42 (changeset_proposals, one row per changeset by primary key —
AC4 in the schema), GET /changesets/{id}/proposal for the review-surface
link, docs/api.md + docs/openapi.json + data-model/deployment/security, and
a [gitsync] push_token_file key that is off by default.

No new dependency and no new .deb runtime requirement: a "push" here is a
contents-API call over net/http, so no git binary, no git library, no
working tree and no ssh key is involved.

Author: brian
Message:
verify: turn the hardware checklist into a command (T-2501)

Hardware validation sat in single digits not because the behaviours were
unproven but because proving one meant a human reading a checklist line,
doing the thing, and writing down what happened. That does not scale, does
not repeat, and cannot be handed to a user who has a cluster and would like
to help.

New internal/verify: 26 checks, one per claim in docs/status-matrix.md §2,
each deciding its own verdict against a real cluster and carrying the API
response, command output or file contents it rests on. `vnproxctl verify
--suite=hardware` is read-only and safe on production; `--out` writes a
signed, timestamped artifact naming the vnprox version, PVE version, kernel
and NIC models the run observed.

Generalised from internal/doctor, keeping the properties that make a
diagnostic worth trusting and enforcing each structurally rather than by
convention:

  - Every check can fail. All I/O arrives through Deps' interfaces, so each
    check has a fixture that breaks it, asserted individually; a check that
    never reaches `fail` under any fixture fails the build with a message
    naming it.
  - A skip is never a pass. Report.OK() requires a pass, not merely no
    failures, so a run in which everything skipped exits non-zero and says
    `0 passed` — the failure that would let a CI job with no cluster
    attached go green forever.
  - A verdict without evidence is malformed. Report.Validate rejects it and
    the CLI refuses to print it.
  - A green run cannot be produced by accident. The suite refuses a mock
    endpoint without --allow-mock, and a run made with the flag is stamped
    in the report so the caveat travels with the document.

AC1 runs both directions against the shipped matrix: a check naming a row
that does not exist fails the build, and so does a row claiming `V` — or
`B` — with nothing behind it. All twelve blocked feature areas are covered.

The destructive interlock is wiring, not policy: without --i-understand no
write client is constructed, so those checks have no path by which to
mutate.

Also:
  - pvemock: both servers now set X-Pvemock, so "am I talking to a mock?"
    is answered by the mock rather than inferred. A cassette replay server
    counts, per T-2502's note.
  - The report's canonical form is enforced on parse, so a byte flipped
    anywhere — including in whitespace — fails verification.
  - Fixed a nondeterministic PF choice in the SR-IOV lifecycle check (map
    range), which was both unreproducible evidence and an unsafe way to
    pick which NIC to provision on.
  - The support-bundle check redacts the session key from its own evidence,
    including on the branch where the bundle leaked it: a report written to
    prove a secret did not escape must not be what lets it escape.

Author: brian
Message:
pvemock: record and replay real PVE traffic (T-2502)

Every fixture in this repository was a guess. T-2108 found four defects
sitting under green unit tests whose fixtures invented the shape the code
expected — the structural consequence of hand-writing each one. This adds
the machinery to observe a response instead.

- internal/redact: the T-1902 support-bundle redactor, extracted unchanged
  so the recorder can apply the same vocabulary (backup -> host -> pvemock
  is an existing edge, so pvemock -> backup would be a cycle, and the
  production PVE client has no business importing the archive layer).
  internal/backup keeps its exported names as thin aliases. New alongside
  the replacement API: a *detection* API (ScanText/ScanJSON) that reports
  findings by field path and rule rather than substituting.
- internal/pvecassette: the on-disk format, the matching rule, the writer
  and the drift comparator. Bodies are stored verbatim so replay is
  byte-identical. Query matching is order-independent and value-sensitive.
- internal/pve: record mode. VNPROX_PVE_RECORD=<dir> plus
  VNPROX_PVE_VERSION writes every request/response pair as a cassette.
  Only the response body is ever passed to the writer: request headers and
  bodies are never collected, in any form.
- internal/pvemock: ReplayServer, a sibling of Server rather than a mode of
  it. It inherits none of Server's ~80 handlers, so an unmatched request
  returns HTTP 599 + ErrNoCassette and fails the test on the spot. There is
  no fallback to configure or forget to disable.
- make record / make record-mock, and cassettes recorded from pvemock under
  internal/pvemock/testdata/cassettes/mock-three-node-vlan/ — named "mock-*"
  because no cassette here came from Proxmox hardware yet.

Two refusals are the point of the card:

Recording a response containing a PVE ticket, a password field or a private
key FAILS THE WRITE and names the field; it is not redacted and written,
because a cassette with a hole where a ticket used to be no longer
describes what PVE returned. The same scan runs on load, so hand-editing a
secret into a cassette fails the suite rather than the review. A
consequence, and a deliberate one: a ticket-auth client cannot record —
its first call is a login, whose response body is a credential.

An unmatched replay request cannot be papered over. Both guards ship with
fixtures that make them fire, and both were mutation-checked: deleting the
scan turns TestWrite_RefusesASecret and TestRecord_TicketLoginIsRefused
red, and adding a fallback to the replay server turns
TestReplay_UnmatchedRequestFailsLoudly red.

Author: brian
Message:
backup: support bundle export (T-1902)

`vnproxctl support-bundle` produces one redacted archive that lets someone
diagnose a stranger's broken install without SSH. It is the gate on Phase 21.

The archive is redacted by construction, not by review:

  * Bundle collectors implement an interface with NO Emits method, so there
    is nowhere to declare an emitted secret class and no flag that could
    make one appear. `secretClasses: []` and `includesKeyMaterial: false`
    are properties of the type, not defaults.
  * Every structured field is declared in bundleFieldSchema with a
    disposition and a written reason it is safe to publish, enforced by a
    reflection walk that fails in both directions — and that REFUSES to let
    a json.RawMessage / any / map field be declared plainly emitted at all.
  * The SQLite store is never included. Derived facts only (schema version,
    migration state, integrity, row counts, the last N redacted
    changesets), read through a new store.InspectReadOnly so that
    diagnosing a failed migration cannot become the thing that migrates it.
  * vnprox.toml and /etc/network/interfaces are re-emitted through per-key
    and per-option allowlists rather than copied — an interfaces(5) file
    can legitimately carry a WireGuard private key.
  * Free-form text (logs, changeset titles, apply output, cert subjects)
    passes a shape-matching redactor; changeset ops are walked by key name
    so a sealed field invented next phase is covered on arrival.

Reuses T-1901 throughout: same archive container, same Staging seam, same
declared secret-class inventory, KindSupportBundle (which Restore already
refuses), and its seeded fixture. The config collector is a SIBLING of the
backup's, not a mode on it.

AC1's scan is lifted from T-1901's including its unsealed-value control,
adapted: a bundle has no store, so there are four must-be-found controls,
one per collection path, and the secret markers are planted in the inputs a
bundle actually reads rather than only in the store.

AC3's three scenarios (wrong PVE credential, port conflict, failed
migration) each read only the archive and each have a healthy control.

Docs: docs/deployment.md "Support bundles", docs/security.md threat model
and summary row, four needs-hardware-validation items.
